body.heading: Words are tools
paragraphs: Words do things. 'You can sit with us' builds a person up. 'Nobody wants you here' knocks a person down. Same mouth, same day — completely different buildings.
You cannot control every word that comes out when you are upset. But you can learn the difference, practice the builders, and repair quickly when a breaker slips out.

body.heading: Builder words
paragraphs: 'You worked really hard on that.' (Noticing effort builds.)
'Do you want help, or do you want to try alone first?' (Asking builds — it respects the person.)
'I like how you…' Finish this sentence about someone today. Specific kindness lands deepest.
'Thank you for…' Gratitude said out loud is the strongest builder of all.

body.heading: Breaker words — and the toothpaste rule
paragraphs: Teasing about how someone looks, learns or talks. Leaving-out words: 'You can't play.' Words said to get a laugh from others at someone's expense.

Here is why breakers matter: words are like toothpaste. Once they squeeze out, you cannot squeeze them back in. You can apologize — and you should — but choosing before speaking is better than repairing after.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Say one builder sentence about each person in your family tonight. Watch what happens to their faces.
2. Think of a breaker word or phrase you have heard at school. What builder words could replace it?

takeaway: Words build or break, and like toothpaste they cannot go back in — so practice builders ('I noticed your effort', 'thank you for…') and repair fast when a breaker slips out.
